intro.heading: The policy is rewritten. Then nobody is sure who has to say yes.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A registered manager rewrites the falls policy after an incident and emails the draft to the deputy. The deputy likes it and replies with a thumbs up. The owner wants the provider's external consultant to look at it too, but that email gets buried. Three weeks on, the old version is still in the shared folder and the new one is in an inbox. Staff are following whichever one they find first. Nobody can say who approved what, or in what order, and the manager has to piece it together from messages.

trail.text: The manager rewrites the falls policy after an incident.
The deputy reads it and replies with a thumbs up.
The owner asks for the external consultant to see it too.
The consultant's email is buried. Nobody chases it.
The old version is still in the shared folder.
Staff use whichever version they find first.
No one can say which version was live on a given date.
"Who approved this policy, and when did staff see it?"

trail_close: The policy was never the problem. The gap is the order of approval and the record of it. Here is how CareStream sets that order, keeps the history and then helps you brief staff.

why.heading: A thumbs up in an email is not a policy approval process

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.a: You decide. An admin adopts the change as a draft. It can then go to a care manager step and, if you switch it on, to an external reviewer. If neither is switched on, it can go straight to live. The care manager step is on by default.

items.q: What does an external reviewer see?
items.a: They get a one off emailed link, with no account needed. They can approve or ask for changes, and a note is required when they ask for changes. The link runs out after 30 days, and you can revoke it or send a new one.

items.q: What if someone only fixes a typo?
items.a: Minor edits such as typos can be applied without the full chain. They are recorded as a tracked change and go straight into the published text.

items.q: Do I get a record of who approved what?
items.a: Yes. You get a version history, with each published edit saved as a read only version. Edited policies move to 2.0, 3.0 and so on. This is the policy version control most managers want when asked which version was live.

items.q: Does it write or change policies on its own?
items.a: No. Gap fixes, wording rewrites and regulation updates are suggestions. They only reach staff after an admin adopts them and the approval chain finishes. Example wording is drafted by our own machine learning, so review it carefully.

items.q: Is it a signed register of who read the policy?
items.a: No. CareStream records reading sessions, which show time spent, how far someone scrolled and whether they pressed Mark as read. It does not collect signatures.

items.q: Once the policy is live, how do staff learn it?
items.a: You allocate an adhoc training module on the topic from the Training screen. Staff complete it in the Staff Hub, and a wrong answer becomes a short lesson they open themselves. You see the picture in Knowledge gaps.

items.q: How do I try it, and what does it cost?
items.a: You can try it free for 14 days by creating a free account. The pricing page shows which plan includes the approval chain.

faqs.heading: Policy sign off in care services, answered

items.q: What is a policy approval process in a care service?
items.a: It is the agreed order of steps a policy change goes through before staff rely on it. In CareStream that can be an admin, a care manager step and an optional external reviewer. See how CareStream works.

items.q: Who approves policies in a care home?
items.a: That is a decision for the provider. Many services have the registered manager, a senior or the owner involved, and some add an outside consultant. CareStream lets you set the steps to match.

items.q: Can policy sign off be skipped for small changes?
items.a: Minor edits such as typos can bypass the chain and are recorded as tracked changes. Real changes to meaning should go through the full order.

items.q: Does the external reviewer need a login?
items.a: No. They receive an emailed link that lasts 30 days. They can approve or request changes, and must add a note if they request changes.

items.q: How do I keep policy version control without a shared folder?
items.a: Each time an edit is published, CareStream saves a read only version and the policy moves to a new major version. The old version stays in the history. Read our guide to version control.

items.q: Is approval the same as staff reading it?
items.a: No. Approval is the leadership decision. Reading is recorded separately as sessions, and training questions show whether staff understood the policy. See adhoc training.

items.q: What does good policy governance look like to an inspector?
items.a: Under Regulation 17 on good governance, systems and processes must be established and operated effectively. Clear approval, kept records and evidence staff understood the policy all support that.

guide.heading: A practical way to set up policy sign off
guide.lede: You do not need a heavy system. You need an order that people follow and a place where the record sits.

paragraphs: Start with a one page note that lists each type of policy and who approves it. Clinical and safeguarding policies might need the registered manager and an external reviewer. A housekeeping procedure might need only a manager. Under Regulation 17 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, a registered person must establish and operate systems to assess, monitor and improve the quality and safety of the services. A written order of approval is one simple part of that.
Staff also need to be ready to follow the result. Regulation 18 says staff must receive the support and training they need to carry out their duties, which is why a briefing after approval matters.

sections.h3: Four steps for a clean policy change
checklist: Draft: adopt or write the change as a draft and leave the live policy alone.
Review: send it through the care manager step and, where needed, the external reviewer.
Publish: check the new version is live and the old one sits in the history.
Brief: allocate a short adhoc module on the topic and look at Knowledge gaps a week later.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the approval order, the version history and the briefing results together, so you can show how a policy became live and whether staff understood it.
